turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll leave these with you before the doctor is in. Best peak flow of the three blows was 340 litres a minute. Pulse 102, oxygen saturation 95 percent, temperature 36.6.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Can we get on with it? I'm wrecked.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry about the wait. Dr Brennan. You do look tired. Tell me what's brought you in.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm after a cold and now I've this wheeze that won't quit, and the chest is—
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tight, is it?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Tight, and I'm whistling every time I breathe out. It's doing my head in.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did the wheezing start?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was up half the night with it. I was meant to be in work this morning and I just couldn't—
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday. It's been there since Thursday. The cold was earlier.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the cold itself, when did that start?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, I haven't a clue. A couple of weeks ago, maybe. I can't remember the day.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it, then or now?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature. Just a stuffed nose at the start, and a cough that hung on.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the cough still with you?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, a bit. Dry mostly. I'm not bringing up anything much.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood at all?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. God, no.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): The breathlessness — is it only when you're moving, or sitting as well?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Sitting here I'm puffed. Stairs at home are worse. I have to stop halfway.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): You've inhalers at home, I take it, with the asthma?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was a child, yeah. Two of them. And I mix the blue and the brown up, that's the whole problem. Half asleep I've no notion which is which.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, we'll untangle it. The blue one is salbutamol, your reliever. The brown is beclometasone, the preventer. Which have you actually been using this week?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue one, again and again. Maybe five, six times a day. Two puffs each time. I think the chemist said they're a hundred micrograms.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Five or six is a fair hammering of it. And the brown beclometasone, are you still on that?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm meant to be on two puffs of the two-hundred microgram one, morning and night. Some days I grab the brown when I'm wheezy, thinking it's the blue, and some days I skip it. I couldn't swear I've taken it right all week.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the twice-a-day preventer, you're not sure you've actually been doing it.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not. No.
[SEG0028] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry, I'll just duck in. The peak flow meter is still out if you want a repeat in a bit.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't. That yoke made me lightheaded. Leave it.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave it so. 340 is a big drop if your usual best is up around—
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Five fifty, when I'm well. They told me that in the clinic years back.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen to your chest.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wheeze through both lungs, louder breathing out. No crackles that I can hear.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that desperate?

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud. This fits an acute flare of your asthma after the virus. The airways are tight, which is why you're living on the blue inhaler and the peak flow is down. I don't think it's a pneumonia — temperature's normal, no crackles, and you're not coughing up anything dirty.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): So just more inhalers? I'm sick of them.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): More than the inhalers. I want to add prednisolone tablets, forty milligrams once a day for five days, by mouth, with food.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days of tablets. Will I be buzzing off them? My sleep is already rotten.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): They can leave you restless or hungry, so take them in the morning, not at night. Finish the five days even if you feel better on day two.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): My head's gone. Which inhaler is which, say it plain.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blue, salbutamol, two puffs when you're wheezy. Use the spacer if you can find it. You shouldn't still be needing it five or six times a day once this settles. If you still need the blue inhaler five or six times a day after a couple of days, come back sooner than planned.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): The spacer's under the bed, I think. Maybe. I don't know.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you find it, use it. The brown one is the beclometasone, two hundred micrograms, two puffs twice a day, every day, even when you feel grand. It will not stop an attack there and then.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Brown is not the rescue one. I've had that backwards for years, so.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any stabbing pain in the chest, separate from the tightness?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just the tight feeling.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not sending you for a chest x-ray today. If you get a fever or start coughing up coloured phlegm, then we would.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): No x-ray unless that happens. Fine.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Start the prednisolone today. Keep the salbutamol for the wheeze, and get properly back on the beclometasone. The prescription will be out at reception.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Am I meant to be off work? I was going to try and—
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): With this much shortness of breath, stay off at least until after the weekend. Rest, drink plenty, and no hard exercise.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): That's ages. Whatever. Fine.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): I want you back here in five days, when you finish the tablets, and we'll recheck the peak flow.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I go downhill before that?
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you can't finish a sentence, or the blue inhaler isn't holding you four hours, go to A&E. Don't sit at home waiting on me. Otherwise it's the five days.
[SEG0057] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll book that five-day review at the desk on your way out.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand, book that.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Just book it. I want to go home and lie down.
[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do that. Take the first prednisolone today with a bit of food if you can. Mind yourself.
